text: Reconnaissance splits into two buckets, and the line between them is simple: does a packet leave your machine and land on infrastructure the target actually owns? If not — if everything you're learning comes from a third party that already holds the data — it's passive. That's why an authorized engagement almost always permits passive recon before the active-testing window even opens, and it's the foundation everything else in this chapter builds on.

Four sources do most of the work. WHOIS tells you who registered a domain, when, and which nameservers are authoritative, even with privacy redaction in place. DNS records — queried against a public resolver, not the target's own — reveal mail providers and authorized sending infrastructure through SPF strings. Certificate Transparency logs are the richest subdomain source available, since every TLS certificate issued gets logged publicly. And job postings, engineering blogs, plus misconfigured public cloud storage round out the picture.

In practice: whois target-company.com returns registrant and registrar data. dig target-company.com MX names the mail provider — Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, or self-hosted. dig target-company.com TXT often surfaces an SPF record listing every IP range authorized to send mail for that domain, which is effectively a free map of egress infrastructure handed to you by the domain's own public DNS.

crt.sh lets you query percent-dot-target-company-dot-com and get back every subdomain anyone has ever requested a certificate for — staging, VPN, internal Jenkins instances — without a single query touching the target's own name servers. A Google dork like site colon s3.amazonaws.com target-company searches Google's index, not the bucket itself, and can surface a world-readable storage bucket holding backups or source code: a serious finding, recorded carefully under the engagement's evidence rules, never downloaded beyond what scope allows.

Notice what all four sources have in common: the target never sees a single request. That's the whole point of passive recon — low risk, high yield, and a head start before anything active ever begins. Next lesson, we turn these individual techniques into a real OSINT methodology, bringing in Shodan, theHarvester, Google dorking as a discipline, and social media footprinting, all still inside the engagement's authorized scope.
